claim: Every's Dan Shipper test: Jev caught 6 of 7 planted writing defects vs Fable 5.1's 7/7, at 0.35s vs 8.83s median per passage and ~580x lower cost; it missed one unexplained action in all three runs.
quote: But Jev caught six of the seven intended defects; Fable caught all seven. One passage proposed “a shared appointment calendar that parents and staff teach together.” ... Jev missed it in all three runs
why: Known lead; direct planted-defect judge test vs frontier model, with a concrete miss. Small n (12 passages). Note Every had pre-launch early access.

claim: CMU arXiv paper (2609.26550, 2026-09-21) found Jev within ~3 points of GPT-6 on RewardBench (92.2 vs 93.5) and HaluEval (87.5 vs 86.7) but 14.6 points behind on JudgeBench (78.6 vs 93.1) and 19.8 behind on style-adversarial RM-Bench (74.8 vs 94.6).
quote: Larger gaps arise when judgments require checking a derivation or resisting an elaborately written wrong answer. On several benchmarks, JEV’s gap to this comparator is concentrated in low-confidence decisions.
why: Most rigorous independent judge eval found (16 comparator judges, blinded human adjudication). Directly names failure modes. Preprint, not peer-reviewed in strict sense.

claim: The CMU paper's frozen confidence cascade (accept confident Jev verdicts, escalate the rest to GPT-6) accepted 53.7% of pairs and scored 92.5% vs 93.1% at 56.8% of the fallback fee, but thresholds failed to transfer across tasks and reference-free prose judging was near chance (52.5-55.0%) with mean max probability ~0.90.
quote: A frozen cascade that accepts confident verdicts and escalates uncertain ones retains 99% of the comparator’s accuracy at lower cost.
why: Calibration evidence plus a direct overconfidence failure (near-chance accuracy with ~0.9 confidence on reference-free prose); figures beyond the abstract came via WebFetch summarizer, verify numbers. Also feeds Q4.

claim: OpenRouter's 2026-09-21 test (jev-1.13-20260917 vs gpt-5.6-luna, 88 HaluEval faithfulness items) found agreement tied (84 vs 83) but Jev better calibrated (Brier 0.043 vs 0.054), while on SummEval long-article open rubrics the LLM judge tracked experts much more closely.
quote: When the rubric is closed and the evidence is included in the request, Jev matched the LLM judge on accuracy. Jev has better-calibrated probabilities... When the rubric is open and reading a whole article is required, the LLM judge follows expert ratings much more closely.
why: Judge calibration with reliability table plus a long-input/open-rubric failure. OpenRouter resells Jev, so has commercial interest; run by Devin agent; small n.

claim: Aman Kumar's ~16,000-call test found Jev level with or ahead of gpt-5.4-mini/gpt-5.6-luna on 3 of 4 public sets (e.g. SST-2 95.7 vs 93.0) but behind on Banking77 (76.0 vs 81.7), and worse than the incumbent small model on whole-document reads.
quote: The longer the input and the fuzzier the labels, or the more business logic the question carries, the more its accuracy and its confidence fall together. On a whole-document read it is worse than the small model we run today, and no prompt fixed that.
why: Large independent classifier test with public scoring repo (github.com/onlyoneaman/jev-eval); directly addresses long-input failure and relevance-filter use ('is this page useful').

claim: In Kumar's production replay, Jev as a 'is this page useful' reject filter agreed with outcomes 97.8% on 1,005 pages and was 100% accurate on the 63% of items where it was confident, but on a 135-row value-extraction gate it fell to 68.6% with probabilities swinging 0.5 between runs.
quote: Jev fires on the mention. It needed about twice as many extraction jobs to match our recall, and its probability swung by 0.5 between runs on the same page.
why: Closest analogue to a research-gatherer relevance scorer: shows where confident-band gating is lossless and where mention-vs-substance confusion breaks it.

claim: MLflow/Databricks test on 30 human-labeled MLflow QA items: Jev 1.13.0 agreed with humans 30/30, same as GPT-5.6 Terra and Luna, ahead of Claude Sonnet 4.6 (27/30) and Opus 4.8 (28/30), at $0.0247 per 1,000 judgments and 369 ms median.
why: Independent judge correctness test with document context; very small n (30) so ceiling effect; Claude configs had reasoning disabled.

claim: LangChain's LangSmith agent-eval test found Jev's quality-score variance 92-913x lower than GPT-5.6 Luna, Terra and Claude Sonnet 4.6, averaging 0.44s and $0.00035 per call ($0.34 total vs $28.17 for Claude).
quote: Jev was dramatically more consistent on continuous scoring. Its quality-score variance was 92–913x lower than GPT-5.6 Luna, Terra, and Claude Sonnet 4.6.
why: Consistency/repeatability evidence for judge use; LangChain is an integration partner (co-hosted webinar with TypeSafe), and authors call it 'narrow' and 'early'.

claim: TypeSafe's own four-workflow benchmark puts Jev at 67.8% vs Claude Opus 5 73.1%, GPT-5.6 Sol 74.1% and Terra 67.9%, scored against a reference built from GPT-6 Astra and Fable 5.1 outputs, which TypeSafe says is the source of its 193.6x faster / 444.6x cheaper claim.
quote: This is where the claims of 193.6x faster, 444.6x cheaper on our home page comes from, and we expect that these are on the higher end of real world gains.
why: Vendor claim baseline; table numbers corroborated via width.ai and dev.to digests; reference is LLM agreement not ground truth, and workflows were built by TypeSafe's own team.

claim: TypeSafe claims RLCD training makes Jev's probabilities calibrated ('higher confidence means higher accuracy') and that Jev 'can't hallucinate', but has published no paper, reward function or calibration methodology.
quote: The reward function, architecture, training procedure, and calibration methodology are all undisclosed.
why: Separates the RLCD calibration claim (vendor) from evidence; dev.to quotes Maio's critique. Arize also calls 'can't hallucinate' an over-reach.

claim: Lindfors' early-access test on 24 Norwegian hearing documents (jev-1.13.0, up to 53,000 chars) got stance 20/24 and found answers at 0.7-1.0 confidence right 97-98% but the 0.3-0.7 band only 34%; longer qualified instructions pushed probabilities toward the middle (calibration error 0.040 to 0.116).
quote: Eleven questions, eleven typed answers with probabilities, 4,995 input tokens, 0.31 seconds. The reference label says `for_with_changes`, so Jev got this one wrong. It also told me it was not sure, and that turned out to be the interesting part.
why: Independent calibration-by-band evidence on non-English, long, nuanced text; prompt-wording sensitivity. Band numbers via WebFetch summary, verify. n=24 small.

claim: Bryo AI's CTO routed 1,565 mostly German supplier emails into 10 categories: Jev 96.4% vs Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite 97.5% and Gemini 3.8 Flash 98.5% (equal-weight 92.0/94.6/96.9), with zero errors in Jev's most confident 85.5% and nearly half wrong below 0.70.
quote: On this set he reports zero errors in Jev's most confident 85.5%, and that nearly half of answers below 70% were wrong.
why: The 1,565-email test named in the brief; secondary aggregator of an author-reported X thread (original not fetched). 364 of 1,565 were AI-written. The 1,500-email Ryan Vogel demo reported no accuracy at all.

claim: JevBench recorded Jev jev-1.13.0 at 62.6% vs Claude Haiku 4.5 81.3% on PhishNChips v5.2 phishing (n=2,000), with phishing recall ranging 43.2% to 98.4% depending on prompt/protocol, and an Amazon ESCI relevance-ranking probe failing four of six pre-registered gates.
quote: Across the runs recorded here Jev ranges from 62.6% to 95.4%. There is no universal Jev accuracy, and our schema has nowhere to store one.
why: Strongest negative independent datapoint plus a relevance-ranking failure (ESCI) directly relevant to gatherer scoring; site authorship anonymous, so lower trust.

claim: An AITA benchmark on 770 Reddit posts put Jev second to Sonnet 5 (weighted Brier 0.369 vs 0.344), 6.3x faster and 62x cheaper, below TypeSafe's claimed 40-200x speedup; decomposing into 8 yes/no questions did worse (41.5-51.5%) than asking directly (53.0%).
quote: In the original seven-setup benchmark, Jev came second, behind Sonnet 5 (Brier score 0.369 vs. 0.344; lower is better). Jev's median call was 6.3× faster than Sonnet's, and 62× cheaper.
why: Independent calibration (Brier) on subjective judgments with CIs; counters vendor speed claim; question decomposition did not help here.
